items.title: Byron Stripling interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: What’s that great thing that Einstein said, he said, “Time is so relative, it’s like you can be with a beautiful girl and the time, one hour seems like a minute; where if you sit on a hot stove for a minute —”

ctx.x: Well the most outlandish thing, especially in the thing for commercial music, is to be asked to improvise. You go why? Improvising is fun to do. Because the people don’t know what they want so if you just are creative, they don’t want that. They want a specific thing. Better to take the heat off yourself, have the writer write it, then you’re in the clear. You just play what’s on there. I hate improvising on jingles. When people start suggesting that, I don’t say anything. Because you get things like this, “Hey”…

whatever. “Yeah, could you play with more colors? Like think of spring. That’s what we’re looking for.” I’m serious. This is what you get. That’s when you start to go look — you almost want to go — and it’s much better to go, “Look, if the writer writes something the pressure’s on him, because I don’t care about colors, I don’t care about spring, I don’t care about fall, I want to just play and get out of here. But those moments are only like fifteen minute periods, maybe like when you’re playing a club date. You…
Just to wrap up here, what’s your impression of the work that goes on at Lincoln Center Jazz and the Smithsonian, well not the Smithsonian, the Carnegie Hall?
